Say that denaturation cannot be undone by cooling, and that enzymes are not killed

Explain a rise in rate with enzyme concentration as more active sites

sheet.howExamined: B1, 1 hour, calculator allowed. Two or three parts of the enzyme question: two factors [2], explain the rise [2], explain the fall [2]-[3], and at Higher an inhibitor part with a letter to choose [1] and a tick table [3]-[4]. Practical B3 is examined in Unit 7 Biology Booklet A (the practical itself) and Booklet B (its theory): times recorded and converted, a mean [1]-[2], a plotted graph [4], the optimum with a reason [2] and a reliability comment [2]. Schemes are point-for-point with a strict accept list: 'denatured' yes, 'killed' no; 'more active sites' yes, 'works faster' no.
traps: Vague answers when two factors are asked for (Summer 2025 B1 F Q5(a))
Saying the enzyme is denatured at LOW temperature — below the optimum it is only slow
Leaving out 'irreversible', or claiming the rate recovers on cooling
Explaining inhibition as denaturation — an inhibitor leaves the enzyme's shape unchanged
Saying an inhibitor reduces the number of active sites; it occupies them
Reading the optimum as the highest point on a graph of TIME (it is the lowest)
Typing a mean as A + B ÷ 2, which divides first (Summer 2024 and Summer 2025 Booklet A)
Leaving a time in minutes and seconds when the column asks for seconds
Answering a reliability question with 'use a better thermometer', which is accuracy
Choosing an awkward scale for the y-axis, or joining the plotted points with a line of best fit when the scheme wants straight lines from point to point (Summer 2024 U7 Booklet A Q1)

noteBlocks.lede: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up a reaction in a living thing. Warm it gently and it works faster; make it too hot, or too acidic, and it stops for good. That is why dough rises in a warm kitchen and why a high fever is dangerous.
can: Name the optimum and say what happens on each side of it.
Explain a rising rate by energy and collisions, and a falling rate by denaturation, in the words the mark scheme rewards.
Read the practical's graph the right way up: the shortest time is the fastest reaction.

noteBlocks.md: Every enzyme has a temperature and a pH at which it works fastest, and on either side of that peak the rate falls away. The two falls are not the same thing, though: too cold only slows the enzyme down, while too hot pulls its shape apart for good. A question that says **explain** wants that difference.

noteBlocks.caption: Two sides, two explanations. Learn them as a pair.

noteBlocks.md: The graph above is the shape every enzyme gives: the rate climbs, peaks, then falls away steeply. The peak is the **optimum**, the temperature at which the reaction runs fastest. The two sides look alike but happen for completely different reasons.

noteBlocks.prompt: The temperature at which an enzyme works fastest is called its ______ .
noteBlocks.explain: The optimum. CCEA's glossary defines it as the value of a factor that allows the reaction to happen at its fastest rate.

noteBlocks.md: **Cold molecules move slowly.** The enzyme and the substrate have less energy, so they meet less often. Fewer collisions means fewer substrate molecules reaching an active site, so the rate is low. Nothing is damaged: warm the tube and the rate climbs back.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why is an enzyme's rate low at 5 °C?
options: Fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate
The enzyme has been denatured
The active site has changed shape
noteBlocks.answer: Fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate
noteBlocks.explain: Nothing is broken at low temperature — the molecules are simply slow. Denaturation only happens above the optimum.

noteBlocks.md: Heat past the optimum and the enzyme molecule changes shape. The **active site** is the part that matters: once its shape has changed, the substrate is no longer complementary to it, cannot fit, and the reaction stops. The change is **irreversible** — that is what *denatured* means.

noteBlocks.alt: Two enzymes side by side. On the left, at the optimum, the substrate's shape matches the notch of the active site. On the right, after heating, the notch is irregular and distorted, and a cross marks that the substrate can no longer fit into it.

noteBlocks.caption: The substrate has not changed. The active site has.

noteBlocks.title: Why cooling does not bring it back
noteBlocks.md: An enzyme is a long chain folded into one exact shape, and that folding is what makes the active site. Heat shakes the chain apart; as it cools it settles into some other folding, and the shape does not return.

noteBlocks.prompt: An enzyme is heated to 70 °C, then cooled back to 37 °C. What happens to its rate?
options: It stays near zero, because the change is irreversible
It returns to what it was at 37 °C
It becomes faster than before
noteBlocks.answer: It stays near zero, because the change is irreversible
noteBlocks.explain: Denaturation is permanent. This is the single most reliable way an exam distinguishes a memorised answer from an understood one.

noteBlocks.md: Both sides arrive as one question about the graph at the top. **(a) Explain why the rate increases between 10 °C and 35 °C. [2] (b) Explain why the rate falls between 45 °C and 60 °C. [3]**
**1.** *As the temperature rises the molecules gain energy and move faster.* Start with what the heat does to the molecules; an answer that jumps straight to collisions has missed a mark.
**2.** *So there are more collisions between the enzyme and the substrate, and more enzyme-substrate complexes form.* That consequence is the second mark in part (a).

noteBlocks.prompt: Part (b) opens “above the optimum the enzyme is denatured”. The change to the active site is then described as ______ .
noteBlocks.explain: Irreversible. Cooling the enzyme does not fold it back, which is why the rate stays near zero.

noteBlocks.md: **3.** *Above the optimum the enzyme is denatured.* Use that word: an enzyme is a molecule, so *killed* and *destroyed* are not on the accept list.
**4.** *The shape of the active site changes, irreversibly.* Which part changes, and that it cannot be undone: two separate ideas, and the pair is rewarded.
**5.** *The substrate is no longer complementary to the active site, so it cannot fit and the reaction stops.* Without it the answer describes a change but not a falling rate.

noteBlocks.prompt: An enzyme with an optimum of pH 7 has almost no rate at pH 2. After “the enzyme is denatured”, what comes next?
options: The active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits
The molecules are too slow to collide
The enzyme recovers at pH 7
noteBlocks.answer: The active site has changed shape, so the substrate no longer fits
noteBlocks.explain: The same ideas as part (b): the active site's shape, and the substrate no longer fitting.

noteBlocks.md: **pH works the same way.** Every enzyme has an optimum pH as well as an optimum temperature, and either side of it the enzyme is denatured. The optima differ widely: a stomach enzyme near pH 2, a mouth enzyme near pH 7.

noteBlocks.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against pH with two bell-shaped curves. The solid curve, enzyme X, peaks at pH 2. The dashed curve, enzyme Y, peaks at pH 7. Both fall to zero either side of their peak.

noteBlocks.md: **Enzyme concentration is different:** nothing is damaged and there is no optimum. More enzyme means **more active sites available**, so more substrate is worked on at once and the rate rises, until every substrate molecule present is already in a complex.

noteBlocks.prompt: The amount of amylase in a tube is doubled, at a fixed temperature. Why does the reaction speed up?
options: There are more active sites available
The substrate has changed shape
The enzyme has a higher optimum
noteBlocks.answer: There are more active sites available
noteBlocks.explain: More enzyme molecules, so more active sites, so more substrate molecules in a complex at any moment.

noteBlocks.title: What the spec prints in bold
noteBlocks.md: **Inhibitors are molecules that fit the active site but are not broken down.** The inhibitor occupies the active site, the substrate is blocked out and the rate falls. The enzyme is **not** denatured: its shape is unchanged.

noteBlocks.alt: An enzyme with a molecule labelled inhibitor sitting inside its active site, and a separate substrate molecule outside marked with a cross to show it cannot get in.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="k74t"><title id="k74t">An inhibitor molecule sitting in the active site, so the substrate is blocked out</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"><path d="M120 200 H240 V128 H212 L200 150 H160 L148 128 H120 Z"/><path d="M144 108 H216 L200 150 H160 Z"/><path d="M340 60 H412 L396 102 H356 Z"/></g><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"><path d="M364 118 l24 24 M388 118 l-24 24"/></g><g font-family="system-ui, sans-serif" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="26" font-weight="600">Inhibitor (Higher Tier)</text><text x="256" y="140">inhibitor: it fits the active site</text><text x="256" y="156">but is not broken down</text><text x="332" y="196">substrate: blocked out,</text><text x="332" y="212">so the reaction rate falls</text><text x="20" y="238" font-size="12">The enzyme is not denatured — its shape is unchanged. The active site is simply occupied.</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Occupied, not damaged. That is the difference between an inhibitor and denaturation.

noteBlocks.prompt: How does an inhibitor reduce an enzyme's rate?
options: It fits the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out
It changes the shape of the active site permanently
It lowers the temperature of the reaction
noteBlocks.answer: It fits the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out
noteBlocks.explain: The specification's own wording. Permanent shape change is denaturation, which is a different thing.

noteBlocks.md: **The method.** Stand a tube of starch solution and a tube of amylase in the water bath until **both reach the bath temperature**, or the run is at the wrong temperature. Put iodine in each well of a spotting tile. Mix, start the stopwatch, and every 30 seconds move a drop into the next well. Iodine stays **blue-black** while starch is present; the first **yellow-brown** well gives the time. Repeat at each temperature.

noteBlocks.explain: (148 + 152) ÷ 2 = 150. Typing 148 + 152 ÷ 2 gives 224, because the calculator divides first — and a mean can never sit outside the two values.

noteBlocks.prompt: From the results, the optimum temperature for this amylase, in °C, is
noteBlocks.explain: 40 °C gave the shortest time, 60 s, so that is where the reaction was fastest.

noteBlocks.md:
· Name the optimum and what happens either side of it.
· Below it: **fewer collisions**, and nothing damaged.
· Above it: **denatured** — the active site changes shape irreversibly and the substrate no longer fits.
· Say what more enzyme does, and what an inhibitor does.
· Read an optimum off a time graph.

Two factors, then the rise explained and the fall explained. In Booklet B it is the practical: times in seconds, a mean, a plotted graph, the optimum. The command words are Explain, Describe, Give a reason, Calculate, Plot and Suggest. Stuck: name the factor, say which way it moves the rate, then give the reason.

steps.working: As the temperature rises the molecules gain energy and move faster.
steps.decision: Start with what the heat does to the molecules. This is the first link, and it is the one candidates skip when they jump straight to 'more collisions'.

steps.working: So there are more collisions between the enzyme and the substrate, and more enzyme-substrate complexes form.
steps.decision: Now the consequence. Summer 2024's examiners named exactly this chain: higher kinetic energy, more successful collisions, more complexes.

steps.working: Above the optimum the enzyme is denatured.
steps.decision: Use the word. 'Killed', 'destroyed' and 'broken' are not on the accept list; denatured is.

options: Because an enzyme is a molecule, not a living thing
Because denatured is a longer word
Because the enzyme dies more slowly than a cell
whyMenu.explain: Only living things can be killed. An enzyme is a protein molecule, so what happens to it is denaturation.

steps.working: The shape of the active site changes, irreversibly.
steps.decision: Say which part changes and that the change cannot be undone. Both are separate ideas and the scheme rewards the pair.

steps.working: The substrate is no longer complementary to the active site, so it cannot fit and the reaction stops.
steps.decision: Finish with the consequence for the substrate. Without this sentence the answer has described a change but not explained a falling rate.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) The molecules gain energy and move faster, so there are more collisions between enzyme and substrate. (b) The enzyme is denatured: the shape of the active site changes irreversibly, so the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.

twin.stem: An enzyme works fastest at pH 7. Explain why its rate is almost zero at pH 2.

accepted: at pH 2 the enzyme is denatured, so the shape of its active site has changed and the substrate can no longer fit

(a) Calculate the mean time. [1]
(b) The class results at six temperatures were 240 s, 150 s, 90 s, 60 s, 105 s and 300 s at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C. State the optimum temperature and give a reason. [2]

figure.alt: A graph of the time for the starch to disappear against temperature from 10 to 60 degrees Celsius: the six class results plotted as crosses and joined by a smooth curve.

steps.decision: Put the addition in brackets before you touch the calculator. Typing 148 + 152 ÷ 2 gives 224, because division is done first.
Check it sits between the two readings. 150 is between 148 and 152, so it is plausible; 224 is outside both and could not be a mean.

options: A mean always lies between the smallest and largest value
A mean is always a whole number
A mean is always smaller than both values
whyMenu.explain: It is the quickest sense check there is, and Summer 2024's examiners recommended it by name.

steps.decision: Read the lowest point of the curve, because this graph plots time. The shortest time is the fastest reaction.

steps.working: because 60 s is the shortest time, so the reaction was fastest at that temperature
steps.decision: Give the reason in the units of the graph. 'Because it is the highest point' would be wrong here — the highest point is the slowest reaction.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 150 s  (b) 40 °C, because it gave the shortest time (60 s) and so the fastest reaction.

items.stem: What does it mean to say an enzyme has been denatured?

options.text: The shape of its active site has changed irreversibly, so the substrate no longer fits
options.feedback: All three ideas are there: the shape, the active site, and irreversible.

options.text: It has been killed
options.feedback: An enzyme is a protein molecule, not a living thing, so it cannot be killed. The word the scheme accepts is denatured.

options.text: It has been used up in the reaction
options.feedback: Enzymes are catalysts and are never used up. Denaturation is a change of shape, not a disappearance.

options.text: Its active site has temporarily changed shape and will recover
options.feedback: The specification says irreversible. Cooling the enzyme down again does not bring the rate back.

items.stem: An enzyme reaction is very slow at 5 °C. Why?
items.skill: Explain the low-temperature side of the curve

options.text: The molecules move slowly, so there are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate
options.feedback: Less energy, slower movement, fewer collisions. Nothing is damaged, which is why warming it up works.

options.text: The enzyme has been denatured by the cold
options.feedback: Denaturation happens above the optimum, not below it. At low temperature the enzyme is intact and simply inactive.

options.text: The active site has shrunk
options.feedback: The active site is unchanged. It is the number of collisions that has fallen.

options.text: There is not enough substrate
options.feedback: Nothing in the question says the substrate has run out; the temperature is what changed.

items.stem: The time for amylase to digest starch was 240 s at 10 °C, 60 s at 40 °C and 300 s at 60 °C. What is the optimum temperature?
items.skill: Read an optimum from a time graph

options.text: 40 °C, because it gave the shortest time
options.feedback: Shortest time means fastest reaction. On a time graph the optimum is the lowest point.

options.text: 60 °C, because it gave the longest time
options.feedback: The longest time is the slowest reaction — at 60 °C the enzyme has been denatured.

options.text: 10 °C, because the enzyme is safest when cool
options.feedback: Safe is not the same as fast. 240 s at 10 °C is four times slower than at 40 °C.

options.text: You cannot tell without the rate
options.feedback: You can: a shorter time is always a faster reaction, so the shortest time marks the optimum.

items.stem: Doubling the concentration of an enzyme doubles the rate. Why?
items.skill: Explain the effect of enzyme concentration

options.text: There are twice as many active sites available
options.feedback: More enzyme molecules, more active sites, more substrate being worked on at once.

options.text: Each enzyme molecule works twice as fast
options.feedback: Each molecule works at the same speed. What changes is how many are working.

options.text: The optimum temperature rises
options.feedback: The optimum is a property of the enzyme and does not move when you add more of it.

options.text: The substrate molecules become smaller
options.feedback: The substrate is unchanged. Only the number of active sites has gone up.

items.stem: An inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction and the rate falls. What has happened? (Higher)

options.text: The inhibitor fits the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out
options.feedback: The specification's own wording. The enzyme itself is unchanged.

options.text: The inhibitor has denatured the enzyme
options.feedback: Denaturation is a change of shape caused by heat or pH. An inhibitor simply occupies the site.

options.text: The inhibitor has been digested into products
options.feedback: It fits, but it is not broken down — that is exactly what makes it an inhibitor and not a substrate.

options.text: The inhibitor lowers the temperature of the mixture
options.feedback: It works on the enzyme, not on the temperature.

context.setting: The opening line of an enzyme question

parts.stem: Give two factors that affect enzyme action.

scheme.for: any two from: temperature / pH / enzyme concentration / substrate concentration / inhibitors — [1] each
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 F Q5(a): vague answers such as 'the conditions' were not credited.

hints: The specification names four: temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and inhibitors.
A vague word such as 'conditions' earns nothing — name the factor.
parts.workedSolution: Temperature and pH are two of them: each one changes how fast the enzyme works, and either can denature it if it goes too far. (Enzyme concentration and inhibitors would do just as well.)

commonErrors.feedback: Summer 2025 examiners reported vague answers here. Name a factor the specification names: temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, inhibitors.

context.setting: A graph of enzyme activity against temperature for a household enzyme

figures.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against temperature rising to an optimum at about 40 degrees Celsius and then falling steeply.

parts.stem: Explain why the rate of reaction increases as the temperature rises from 10 °C to 30 °C.

accepted: the molecules have more energy and move faster, so there are more collisions between enzyme and substrate

scheme.for: the molecules gain (kinetic) energy and move faster
so there are more collisions between the enzyme and the substrate / more enzyme-substrate complexes form

hints: Two links: what heat does to the molecules, and what that does to the meetings between them.
parts.workedSolution: Warming gives the enzyme and substrate molecules more energy, so they move faster and collide more often. More collisions means more enzyme-substrate complexes form each second, so the rate rises.

commonErrors.feedback: 'Less collisions' is the wrong direction and the wrong word. Warming increases the number of collisions per second.

parts.stem: Explain why the rate falls above 45 °C.

accepted: the enzyme is denatured: the shape of the active site changes irreversibly so the substrate no longer fits

scheme.for: the enzyme is denatured
the shape of the active site changes (irreversibly)
so the substrate is no longer complementary to it and cannot fit

hints: Three marks means three separate ideas: the word, the part that changes, and the consequence.
Enzymes are molecules, so never write 'killed'.
parts.workedSolution: Above 45 °C the enzyme is denatured. The shape of the active site changes irreversibly, so the substrate is no longer complementary to it, cannot fit, and the reaction cannot be catalysed.

commonErrors.feedback: An enzyme is a protein molecule, not a living thing. Replace 'killed' with 'denatured' and the first mark is safe.

context.setting: Two enzymes from different parts of the gut compared on one pH graph

figures.alt: A graph of rate of reaction against pH from 0 to 14 for two enzymes, X as a solid curve and Y as a dashed curve, each rising to a single peak and then falling.

parts.stem: Use the graph to state the optimum pH of enzyme X.

scheme.for: pH 2 (accept 1.5–2.5)

hints: The optimum is the pH at the top of that enzyme's curve.
parts.workedSolution: The solid curve peaks at pH 2.

parts.stem: State the optimum pH of enzyme Y.

scheme.for: pH 7 (accept 6.5–7.5)

hints: Read the dashed curve this time.
parts.workedSolution: The dashed curve peaks at pH 7.

commonErrors.feedback: That is enzyme X's optimum. Check which curve the question names — solid or dashed — before reading across.

parts.stem: Explain why enzyme X has almost no activity at pH 7.

accepted: pH 7 is far from its optimum so it has been denatured and the shape of its active site has changed

scheme.for: pH 7 is well away from its optimum, so the enzyme is denatured
the shape of its active site has changed, so the substrate no longer fits

hints: The same two ideas as for temperature: denatured, then the active site.
parts.workedSolution: pH 7 is a long way from enzyme X's optimum of pH 2, so the enzyme is denatured: the shape of its active site has changed and the substrate can no longer fit into it.

context.setting: Two tubes with the same starch solution but different amounts of amylase

parts.stem:
Tube 1 and tube 2 hold the same volume of starch solution at the same temperature. Tube 2 holds twice as much amylase as tube 1.
The starch disappears sooner in tube 2.
Explain why.

accepted: tube 2 has more enzyme molecules so more active sites are available and more starch can be digested at once

scheme.for: tube 2 contains more enzyme molecules
so more active sites are available and more substrate is being broken down at the same time

hints: The enzymes have not changed — there are just more of them.
The phrase the scheme wants is 'more active sites'.
parts.workedSolution: Tube 2 contains twice as many amylase molecules, so twice as many active sites are available. More starch molecules are in an enzyme-substrate complex at any moment, so the starch is digested in a shorter time.

commonErrors.feedback: Each enzyme molecule works at the same speed. What has changed is the number of active sites available.

context.setting: An enzyme drawn with three molecules, one of which is an inhibitor

figures.alt: An enzyme with an inhibitor molecule sitting in the notch in its surface, and a substrate molecule of the same shape outside it, marked with a cross.

parts.stem: Explain how an inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction.

accepted: the inhibitor fits into the active site but is not broken down, so the substrate cannot enter

scheme.for: the inhibitor fits into the active site
but it is not broken down, so the substrate is blocked out and fewer complexes form

hints: The specification's wording is 'molecules that fit the active site but are not broken down'.
parts.workedSolution: An inhibitor has a shape that lets it fit into the active site, but the enzyme cannot break it down, so it stays there. While it is in place the substrate cannot enter, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and the rate falls.

commonErrors.feedback: Denaturation changes the enzyme's shape. An inhibitor leaves the enzyme unchanged and simply occupies the site.

parts.stem: Give one way in which the effect of an inhibitor is different from the effect of heating an enzyme above its optimum.

accepted: the enzyme is not denatured by an inhibitor, so its shape is unchanged

scheme.for: the inhibitor does not denature the enzyme / the shape of the active site is unchanged
accept: removing the inhibitor can restore activity, whereas denaturation is irreversible

hints: One is a blocked site; the other is a changed site.
parts.workedSolution: An inhibitor does not denature the enzyme: the active site keeps its shape and is only occupied, whereas heating above the optimum changes that shape irreversibly.

context.setting: Two groups timing the same reaction in minutes and seconds

parts.stem:
Group A recorded a time of 2 minutes 28 seconds.
Convert this time to seconds.
hints: Multiply the minutes by 60 before adding the seconds.

commonErrors.feedback: 228 treats the minutes as hundreds. One minute is 60 seconds, so 2 minutes is 120 seconds.

parts.stem:
Group B recorded 152 s for the same temperature.
Calculate the mean time for the two groups.
Show your working out.

scheme.examinerNote: Correct answer is worth [2]. A mean outside the two values cannot be right.

hints: Add first, then divide — put the addition in brackets on the calculator.

commonErrors.feedback: 224 comes from typing 148 + 152 ÷ 2, which divides before it adds. Summer 2024 and Summer 2025 examiners both named this. A mean must lie between the two readings.

context.setting: A class investigating how temperature affects the time amylase takes to digest starch

figures.alt: A water bath holding separate tubes of starch solution and amylase with a thermometer, a spotting tile with a drop of reagent in each well, and a stopwatch.

parts.stem: Name the reagent placed in the wells of the spotting tile, and give the colour it turns while starch is still present.

scheme.for: iodine (solution)
blue-black

hints: The reagent is the starch test from section 1.3.
parts.workedSolution: Iodine solution, which turns blue-black while starch is still present.

commonErrors.feedback: Those two test for sugar and protein. The starch test is iodine solution, turning yellow-brown to blue-black.

parts.stem: Describe how the student would find the time taken for the starch to be digested at one temperature.

accepted: mix the warmed solutions, start the stopwatch, and every 30 seconds test a drop with iodine until it stays yellow-brown

scheme.for: mix the starch and amylase and start the stopwatch
every 30 seconds remove a drop of the mixture and add it to a well of iodine solution
accept: test a sample at regular intervals

scheme.for: record the time when the iodine first stays yellow-brown, showing no starch is left

hints: Three steps: mix and start, sample at regular intervals, stop at the colour change.
Say what the end point looks like — 'until it is done' is not a result.
parts.workedSolution: Mix the warmed starch solution with the warmed amylase and start the stopwatch. Every 30 seconds remove a drop of the mixture with a dropping pipette and add it to the next well of iodine solution. Record the time at which the iodine first stays yellow-brown, which shows all the starch has been digested.

commonErrors.feedback: The method has no end point, so there is nothing to time. Say what the iodine looks like when the starch has gone.

parts.stem:
Before mixing, the student leaves both tubes standing in the water bath for five minutes.
Give a reason for this.

accepted: so that both solutions reach the temperature of the water bath before the reaction starts

scheme.for: so both solutions reach the temperature of the water bath before they are mixed
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 Booklet A: most candidates saw that the enzyme and substrate need time to warm to the set temperature.

hints: Think about what the investigation is measuring, and when the clock starts.
parts.workedSolution: So that the enzyme and the substrate are both at the bath temperature before the reaction starts; otherwise part of the timed reaction would happen at the wrong temperature.

parts.stem: State the independent variable, the dependent variable and one control variable for this investigation.

accepted: independent: the temperature; dependent: the time for the starch to be digested; control: the volume or concentration of amylase

scheme.for: independent: temperature (of the water bath)
dependent: the time taken for the starch to be digested
control: the volume and concentration of amylase / of starch / the pH / the size of each drop
scheme.examinerNote: Naming the independent variable as the control earns nothing (research 03 §7.4).

hints: Independent = changed on purpose. Dependent = measured. Control = deliberately kept the same.
parts.workedSolution: Independent: the temperature of the water bath. Dependent: the time taken for the iodine to stop turning blue-black. Control: the volume and concentration of the amylase (and of the starch), kept the same at every temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: Temperature is the variable being changed, so it cannot also be the one held constant. Name something else that would affect the time, such as the concentration of amylase.

context.setting: Class results for the amylase-and-starch investigation at six temperatures

columns: Time for the starch to disappear / s
data.caption: Class results, one run at each temperature

data.yLabel: Time for the starch to disappear / s
data.caption: Grid for the plot

parts.stem:
At 60 °C the starch had still not disappeared after 5 minutes.
Complete the results table.

scheme.examinerNote: 5 × 60 = 300 s; the column heading already gives the unit.

hints: The column is in seconds, so convert the five minutes first.
parts.workedSolution: 5 minutes = 5 × 60 = 300 s.

commonErrors.feedback: The column heading asks for seconds. Five minutes is 300 s.

parts.stem: Plot the results on the grid and join the points with straight lines.

scheme.for: suitable use of the printed scale, with a sharp pencil
all six points plotted correctly (within half a small square)
points joined with ruled straight lines
the curve shows a clear minimum between 30 °C and 50 °C

hints: This graph is not a straight-line relationship, so a line of best fit is not what is wanted here — join the points.
Check the point at 60 °C is at 300 s, not 5.
parts.workedSolution: Plot (10, 240), (20, 150), (30, 90), (40, 60), (50, 105) and (60, 300), then join them with ruled straight lines. The result is a V-shaped curve with its lowest point at 40 °C.

commonErrors.feedback: Summer 2024 examiners reported marks lost for an unsuitable scale. Use at least half the grid: the times run from 60 s to 300 s, so a 0-300 axis in steps of 50 fits well.

parts.stem: State the optimum temperature for this enzyme and give a reason for your answer.

accepted: 40 °C, because it gave the shortest time so the reaction was fastest

scheme.for: because it gave the shortest time / the fastest reaction
reject: because it is the highest point
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 Booklet A: most candidates saw that the optimum was the temperature giving the minimum time.

hints: This graph plots time, so the fastest reaction is the lowest point.
parts.workedSolution: 40 °C. It gave the shortest time, 60 s, so the starch was digested fastest at that temperature.

commonErrors.feedback: 60 is either the time in seconds or the temperature with the longest time. The optimum is where the time is shortest, which is 40 °C.

parts.stem: Explain how the class could improve the reliability of these results.

accepted: repeat each temperature several times and take a mean

scheme.for: repeat the timing at each temperature
and calculate a mean / compare the repeats to check they agree
scheme.examinerNote: Reliability is repeats and agreement; a better thermometer would be accuracy.

hints: Reliability is about repeating and comparing, not about better equipment.
parts.workedSolution: Repeat the timing at least three times at each temperature and calculate a mean. If the repeats agree closely the results can be trusted, and an odd reading shows up so it can be left out.

commonErrors.feedback: A better thermometer improves accuracy. Reliability is improved by repeating the measurement and checking the repeats agree — Summer 2025 Booklet B reported the two being confused.

context.setting: Two tubes of the same enzyme and substrate, one with an inhibitor added

parts.stem: Explain, in terms of active sites, why tube 2 produced very little product.

accepted: the inhibitor molecules fit into the active sites but are not broken down, so fewer substrate molecules can enter and fewer complexes form

scheme.for: the inhibitor molecules fit into the active sites
but they are not broken down, so they stay there
so fewer substrate molecules can enter an active site and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form

hints: Three marks means three separate ideas: it fits, it stays, the substrate is shut out.
parts.workedSolution: The inhibitor molecules have a shape that lets them fit into the active sites of the enzyme. They are not broken down, so they stay in place. While they are there, substrate molecules cannot enter the active sites, so far fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and very little product is made.

commonErrors.feedback: The enzyme is not denatured — its shape is unchanged. It is the active site being occupied that stops the reaction.

parts.stem:
Complete the sentences by writing **greater**, **less** or **the same** in each gap.

The number of successful collisions between substrate and enzyme in tube 2 was ______ than in tube 1.
The number of active sites in tube 2 was ______ as in tube 1.
The rate of product formation in tube 2 was ______ than in tube 1.

scheme.for: less
the same
scheme.examinerNote: The inhibitor blocks active sites but does not destroy them; the number of active sites is unchanged.

scheme.for: less

hints: The enzyme itself has not changed, so ask what has: which sites are free, not how many exist.
parts.workedSolution: Fewer substrate molecules reach a free active site, so successful collisions are less. The enzyme is unchanged, so the number of active sites is the same. Less product forms per minute, so the rate is less.

commonErrors.feedback: The middle gap is the trap. An inhibitor occupies active sites; it does not remove them, so the enzyme still has the same number.

context.setting: A student planning the amylase investigation from scratch

parts.stem:
A student is given amylase solution, starch solution, iodine solution, a spotting tile, water baths at different temperatures and the usual laboratory apparatus.
Describe how she should investigate how temperature affects the action of amylase.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: place a drop of iodine solution in each well of the spotting tile
stand separate tubes of starch solution and amylase in the water bath and leave them to reach its temperature
mix the two solutions and start the stopwatch
every 30 seconds transfer a drop of the mixture to the next well of iodine
record the time when the iodine first stays yellow-brown instead of turning blue-black
repeat the whole method at several different temperatures
keep the volumes and concentrations of starch and amylase the same each time, and repeat each temperature to find a mean

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Write it as ordered sentences with capital letters and full stops; that is part of the band judgement.
Two things are easy to forget: warming the tubes before mixing, and saying what the end point looks like.
parts.workedSolution: Put a drop of iodine solution into each well of the spotting tile. Stand a tube of starch solution and a tube of amylase in the water bath at the first temperature and leave them for five minutes so both reach that temperature. Mix the two solutions and start the stopwatch. Every 30 seconds remove a drop of the mixture and add it to the next well. While starch remains the iodine turns blue-black; record the time at which it first stays yellow-brown. Repeat the whole method at several temperatures, keeping the volumes and concentrations of starch and amylase the same each time, and repeat each temperature so that a mean time can be calculated.

commonErrors.feedback: The method never says how you know the reaction has finished, so there is nothing to time. The end point — iodine staying yellow-brown — is one of the seven indicative points.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoibhín is asked: 'Two groups timed the same reaction at 20 °C. Group A recorded 148 s and Group B recorded 152 s. Calculate the mean time. Show your working out. [2]'
Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The two readings have to be added before anything is divided, so the addition needs brackets: (148 + 152) ÷ 2. As written, the calculator divides 152 by 2 first and then adds it to 148.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks, but the repair is one pair of brackets. There is also a free check: a mean always lies between the two values it came from, and 224 is larger than both readings. Summer 2024 and Summer 2025 examiners both reported this exact keying error in the Booklet A biology task and asked candidates to look at whether a result seems reasonable.

prompts.prompt: What is the optimum for an enzyme?
prompts.answer: The value of a factor — temperature or pH — at which the reaction happens at its fastest rate.

An irreversible change in the shape of an enzyme, so that its active site is no longer complementary to the substrate and it cannot catalyse the reaction. Caused by high temperature or by pH away from the optimum.

prompts.prompt: Why is an enzyme reaction slow at 5 °C? (Not 'the enzyme is denatured'.)
prompts.answer: The molecules have less energy and move more slowly, so there are fewer collisions between enzyme and substrate.

prompts.prompt: Why does more enzyme give a faster reaction?
prompts.answer: There are more enzyme molecules, so more active sites are available and more substrate is being broken down at the same time.
A molecule that fits into the active site of an enzyme but is not broken down, so it stops the substrate entering and reduces the rate.

prompts.prompt: Give the method for Prescribed Practical B3 in five steps.
prompts.answer: 1 Iodine in the wells of a spotting tile. 2 Warm separate tubes of starch and amylase in the water bath. 3 Mix and start the stopwatch. 4 Every 30 s test a drop with iodine. 5 Record the time when it first stays yellow-brown, then repeat at other temperatures.

prompts.prompt: A graph plots the TIME for a reaction against temperature. Where is the optimum?
prompts.answer: At the lowest point — the shortest time is the fastest reaction. On a rate graph it would be the highest point instead.

prompts.prompt: How do you calculate a mean on a calculator without the BODMAS error?
prompts.answer: Put the addition in brackets: (A + B) ÷ 2. Then check the answer lies between A and B.
